items.title: 66100_Bud Freeman oral history interview
items.q: we had Cliff Leeman on drums and Jess and Cliff didn't hit

ctx.x: But I am sure that he would be very tempted if he actually realized and knew that the things were at the stage that they are, I think he would be tempted.

Yes, just on the publicity he's gotten, you know, making a comeback and of course, the New Yorker article, which is a tremendous piece. That is big international stuff, I think he would get the greatest surprise of his life, because when we played in the trio, we played -- we did a duet date since we were recording a duet, we had Cliff Leeman on drums and Jess and Cliff didn't hit -- they didn't get on too well together, so we decided without offending Cliff, who is a super drummer, that we would do a session…

bers, we played Don't Blame Me as a ballad and some blues in F in a fast tempo, and I couldn't -- Jess got a standing ovation and I couldn't get him to stand up, he was so scared, but he played beautifully.

items.title: 68087_Cliff Leeman oral history interview
items.q: and he used Bud Freeman on tenor

ctx.x: When the wonderful, great piano player, Ralph Sutton, visited my house, he looked at the picture and commented, "Where were your sixguns, Cliff?" and I said "Security wouldn't allow me".

And I need an insertion here. That was the Bicentennial that we were playing -- I left out the word 'bi', which was of course, nationwide -- rather, our nation's great celebration. I noticed that in playing this back, that I had talked into this machine, this fool machine here for 10 or 15 minutes about the Lawson-Haggard band, and upon our recording with a larger group, and I forgot to push all the proper buttons. So it was deleted. However, Bob Haggard and Lawson in doing the arrangements, wanted to enlarge…
And of course we added George Burns, who was working at that time on the Hit Parade. So I hope this might be inserted -- it's of importance to me.
